pages.title: The Living AI Book
paragraphs: How clever computers learn, what they can do, and how we can shape what comes next.

pages.title: Inside this book
paragraphs: Choose a chapter below, or use the arrow keys to turn one spread at a time.

pages.title: A book that can grow
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is changing quickly. This book explains the big ideas in simple language, then adds a shelf of recent announcements from official sources. The explanations are the sturdy map; the news shelf is the part that keeps moving.

pages.title: How to read it
paragraphs: Pick a chapter from the menu. Try the small activities, follow the source links, and ask questions. You do not need to be a computer expert. Curiosity is enough to get started.

pages.title: A helpful rule
paragraphs: AI can be useful, but it can also make mistakes. Treat it like a clever helper that needs checking—not like an all-knowing grown-up.

pages.title: AI, or SI?
paragraphs: The established name for this field is artificial intelligence, or AI. “SI” by itself is ambiguous, and “smart intelligence” is not the formal name of the field. You may also hear AGI (artificial general intelligence) or ASI (artificial superintelligence), ideas about much broader or greater-than-human abilities that remain hypothetical. Today's AI tools are not proof that AGI or ASI exists.

pages.title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Pause and explore this idea in your own way.
pages.callout: Open the prompt playground and make a vague request clearer. The book builds the prompt on your device; it does not send it to an AI company.

pages.title: A machine that can do clever-looking tasks
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is a name for computer programs that do tasks we often connect with human thinking. An AI might spot objects in a picture, suggest a route, translate a sentence, or help draft a story.

pages.title: Not a tiny person in the computer
paragraphs: An AI program does not have a human body or human life. It can use words that sound friendly, but that does not mean it has feelings, memories, or experiences like you do.

pages.title: A simple example
paragraphs: A photo app can learn clues that often appear in pictures of cats, such as ears, eyes, and fur. It uses those clues to make a guess. It can still mistake a toy cat for a real one!

pages.title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Pause and explore this idea in your own way.
pages.callout: Look at three pictures of the same kind of thing. What clues would help a computer tell them apart? What tricky picture might fool it?

pages.title: Examples are practice
paragraphs: Imagine teaching a computer to sort apples and oranges. You show it many labelled examples. During training, it adjusts its internal settings to get better at matching pictures with labels.

pages.title: Practice data matters
paragraphs: If most practice pictures show shiny red apples, the computer may struggle with a green apple. If examples leave out important people or situations, its answers may work less well for them.

pages.title: It is not learning exactly like you
paragraphs: A computer adjusts numbers in a model. It does not go outside, taste fruit, or understand the experience of eating an apple. The word “learn” is useful, but machine learning is different from a child's learning.

pages.title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Pause and explore this idea in your own way.
pages.callout: Make a pretend training set for sorting shoes and hats. Include unusual examples too—like a hat shaped like a shoe. What could go wrong if all your examples look alike?

pages.kicker: 3. How does a language model write?
pages.title: A very good next-piece guesser
paragraphs: A large language model, or LLM, studies patterns in lots of text. When asked to write, it repeatedly guesses what piece of text should come next. A piece can be a whole word or only part of one.

pages.title: A tiny pretend example
paragraphs: After “The dog wagged its…”, a person might guess “tail.” A language model compares patterns it learned and picks a likely next piece. It can keep going to make a sentence or a much longer answer.

pages.title: A smooth answer can still be wrong
paragraphs: The model is making a pattern-based answer, not checking every sentence against a perfect fact book. It can sound sure and still invent a name, number, or explanation. Check important facts with a trusted person or reliable source.

pages.title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Pause and explore this idea in your own way.
pages.callout: Finish “For my science project, I want to learn about…” in three different ways. Notice how a few extra words change what kind of answer would be useful.

pages.title: Big moments, not every moment
paragraphs: AI has a long story with many people, ideas, and inventions. Here are a few milestones—not a complete list. Each one built on earlier work, and none happened all by itself.

pages.title: Turing asks a big question
paragraphs: Mathematician Alan Turing described an “imitation game” to explore how we might judge a machine by its conversation. It started a lasting discussion about machines and thinking.

links.label: Turing's paper, Computing Machinery and Intelligence

pages.title: AI becomes a research field
paragraphs: At a summer workshop at Dartmouth College, researchers helped establish artificial intelligence as a field of study. The name “artificial intelligence” was used in the workshop proposal.

links.label: Dartmouth: The research conference where AI began

pages.title: ELIZA chats using written rules
paragraphs: Joseph Weizenbaum described ELIZA, an early computer program that replied to typed messages using patterns and rules. Its replies could feel conversational, even though the program did not understand like a person.

links.label: Weizenbaum's paper on ELIZA (ACM Digital Library)

pages.title: Deep Blue wins a chess match
paragraphs: IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. It was a remarkable chess achievement—but Deep Blue was designed to play chess, not to do every kind of human thinking.

pages.title: Neural networks make waves in image contests
paragraphs: AlexNet, a deep neural network, achieved a major result in the ImageNet image-recognition challenge. It helped draw attention to what neural networks could learn from many labelled examples.

links.label: Krizhevsky et al., 2012 paper (ACM reprint): ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

pages.title: The Transformer idea is published
paragraphs: Researchers introduced the Transformer, a new way for computers to work with relationships between pieces of language. It became an important building block for many later language models.

pages.title: ChatGPT opens to the public
paragraphs: OpenAI introduced ChatGPT as a research preview in November. Many people could try a conversational AI tool directly, helping make chat with language models a familiar experience.

pages.title: Machine-learning pioneers receive a Nobel Prize
paragraphs: The Nobel Prize in Physics recognized John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for discoveries and inventions that helped make machine learning with artificial neural networks possible.

links.label: Nobel Prize: They used physics to find patterns in information

pages.title: Helpful jobs for AI
paragraphs: AI can help sort photos, suggest music, translate short messages, read text aloud, find patterns in medical images, or help a person brainstorm. A human should still make important choices and check the result.

pages.title: A schoolwork helper
paragraphs: You could ask for a tricky science idea to be explained in simpler words, then compare the explanation with your textbook. Use help to understand—not to pretend someone else's work is yours.

pages.title: A family helper
paragraphs: A family could ask an AI for a list of picnic ideas or a first draft of a packing checklist. A grown-up should check the weather, food safety, and any important details.

pages.title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Pause and explore this idea in your own way.
pages.callout: Use the prompt playground to give an AI helper a clear job, useful details, and a limit. A more careful question often gets a more useful answer.

pages.title: The prompt playground
paragraphs: A prompt is an instruction for an AI tool. Build a clearer example and see how small details can guide an answer.

pages.title: Different tools, different jobs
paragraphs: These are examples of well-known AI products and automation tools—not a ranking or a promise that every feature is available to everyone. Products change, so check each official site for current details. Ask a trusted adult before creating an account, sharing information, or connecting services.

pages.title: Which tool for which task?
paragraphs: These tools have different jobs. Pick one that fits your task, and check its answer or result.

applications.name: ChatGPT
applications.description: A chat-based helper for questions, writing ideas, explanations, and other tasks. It can make mistakes, so check important answers.
applications.use_when: You want to ask questions, understand a topic, or brainstorm a first draft.

applications.name: Google Gemini
applications.description: Google's AI assistant can help people explore questions and work with different kinds of information. Available features depend on the account, device, and region.
applications.use_when: You want an AI assistant for questions and help exploring information.

applications.name: Claude
applications.description: An AI assistant from Anthropic that can help with questions, writing, and working with files. Treat its answers as suggestions to review, not guaranteed facts.
applications.use_when: You want help discussing ideas, drafting text, or reviewing documents.

applications.name: Lovable
applications.description: A tool for creating website and app prototypes from written instructions. A real app still needs people to test it, protect user information, and check its code.
applications.use_when: You want to turn an app idea into a first website or app prototype.

applications.name: n8n
applications.description: A tool for connecting apps and services into automated workflows. It is more like building a set of linked steps than chatting with a general AI assistant.
applications.use_when: You want different apps to pass information or carry out repeatable steps automatically.

pages.callout: The website and its features may change. Ask a trusted adult before signing up or sharing personal information.

pages.kicker: 7. Be a smart and safe AI user
pages.title: Keep private things private
paragraphs: Do not put passwords, your home address, private photos, school records, or another person's secrets into an AI tool. Ask a parent, guardian, or teacher before trying a new service.

pages.title: Check before you share
paragraphs: AI can make up facts or create pictures and voices that look real. For health, money, safety, or school facts, check a reliable source and ask a trusted adult. Do not forward surprising claims just because they look polished.

pages.title: Be fair and kind
paragraphs: AI can repeat unfair patterns found in its examples. Think about who might be missing or treated unfairly. Never use AI to bully, trick, or embarrass somebody.

pages.title: People are responsible
paragraphs: A person who uses or shares an AI result is still responsible for the choice. AI can suggest; people need to decide whether the suggestion is safe, fair, and true.

pages.title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Pause and explore this idea in your own way.
pages.callout: Before using an AI answer, ask: Who made this? Could it be wrong? Is it private? Who could it affect? Who can help me check?

pages.title: What might become possible?
paragraphs: People are exploring AI tutors that change their explanations, tools that help doctors study information, robots that assist with repetitive jobs, and creative tools for music, art, and games. These are areas people are working on—not promises that every idea will work.

pages.title: Better questions for the future
paragraphs: Will a tool help people learn, or just do their work for them? Who checks mistakes? Does it protect private information? Can people choose not to use it? Who benefits, and who might be left out?

pages.title: You can help shape it
paragraphs: The future of AI is not decided by computers alone. Students, families, teachers, scientists, artists, and communities can all help decide which tools are worth building and what rules they should follow.

pages.title: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Pause and explore this idea in your own way.
pages.callout: Invent one AI helper for a real problem. Draw or describe it, explain who it helps, and write one safety rule it must follow.
